outline.description: This chapter establishes the foundational context of the dispute, identifying the parties, the nature of the technology involved (Passive Intermodulation or PIM), and the procedural history leading to the Federal Circuit's review. It details the specific patents in suit ('134 and '775), the jury's initial findings of validity and infringement, and the significant damages award that prompted the appeals.
subtopics: Parties and Technology Background: Finesse Wireless vs. AT&T/Nokia regarding PIM mitigation in radios
Patent Scope: Summary of U.S. Patents No. 7,346,134 and 9,548,775
Procedural Posture: Jury verdict, JMOL motions, and the district court's denial of relief
Standard of Review: Application of Fifth Circuit law for JMOL and substantial evidence review

outline.description: This section provides a deep dive into why the court reversed the denial of Judgment as a Matter of Law (JMOL) regarding the '134 patent. It focuses on Claim 1's requirement to sample both 'signals of interest' and 'interference generating signals.' The chapter analyzes the fatal flaws in Plaintiff's expert testimony, specifically regarding the temporal impossibility of sampling signals that are generated post-sampling.
subtopics: Claim Construction Limitation: Requirement to sample a passband containing both signal types simultaneously
Expert Testimony Analysis: Dr. Wells' identification of 'modeled PIM path' versus actual physical signal paths
Temporal Impossibility Argument: Why interference signals cannot exist at the moment of sampling by the RF ADC
Evidentiary Insufficiency: How contradictory expert testimony fails to meet the burden of proof for literal infringement

outline.chapter_title: Analysis of '775 Patent Infringement Claims and Prosecution History
outline.description: This chapter examines the reversal concerning the '775 patent, addressing two primary issues: whether amending claims to specify 'three signals' constituted a surrender (disavowal) of devices using only two unique signals, and whether there was sufficient evidence that seven specific digital multiplications occurred. It contrasts legal arguments regarding prosecution history estoppel with factual deficiencies in mapping technical operations.
subtopics: Prosecution History Estoppel: Analyzing whether amending 'two or three' to 'three' disclaimed two-signal embodiments
The Seven Multiplication Requirement: Dissecting Claim 1(d)'s mathematical constraints
Mapping Failure: The disconnect between Nokia's technical documentation (showing three distinct ops/modulus) and the seven claimed multiplications
New Evidence Barred on Appeal: Why Finesse's attempt to introduce new mappings at oral argument was insufficient

outline.chapter_title: '775 Patent Legal Standards on Signal Identification
outline.description: (Note: Integrated into Chapter 3 above in some outlines, but separated here for clarity on specific legal standards applied to signal definitions). This chapter clarifies the district court's construction that 'three signals' need not be unique but must be separately identifiable. It explores how this construction interacts with the factual record to determine if using x1, x2, and a copy of x2 satisfies the claim language versus requiring three distinct unique inputs.
subtopics: 'Separately Identifiable' vs. 'Unique': Understanding claim construction boundaries established at summary judgment
Application to Accused Device: Evaluating if using two unique inputs plus a derived copy meets statutory requirements under current construction
**Correction/Refinement**: Clarification that while claim scope wasn't surrendered, factual proof still failed due to missing multiplication steps.
